axes.question: Which public budgets and instruments support the relevant actors?
Who can apply and how are projects selected?
What activities and outputs are public funds designed to purchase or support?
Are relationships grants, procurement, decentralised subsidies or other vehicles, and who controls them?
What reporting, evaluation and control duties accompany the funding?
Does public funding establish editorial/moderation command or political/electoral effect?

causal.gap: The chain is well evidenced through program design, selection and funded capacity/outputs, but not as a general chain to specific lawful-content removal, persuasion or electoral outcome.
causal.limit: Public funding can shape eligible agendas and capacity without proving downstream command or political effect.
causal.mechanism: public objective -> call/eligibility -> selection/grant or procurement -> funded capacity -> specified output/activity -> audience/platform/institutional exposure -> possible moderation or opinion effect -> possible political/electoral result

claims.claim: France and the EU maintain a real, recurring and materially funded ecosystem of associations, consortia and service providers working on anti-hate, radicalisation prevention, media literacy and disinformation resilience.
claims.gap: The corpus is a mechanism sample, not a complete beneficiary-level census.

claims.claim: Funding rules can shape capacity and agenda at the program level by defining eligible themes, target groups, expected deliverables and reporting obligations.
claims.gap: Programmatic alignment does not establish instruction over each downstream publication or moderation decision.

claims.claim: The financing architecture is plural rather than unitary: national calls, decentralised grants, multi-year agreements, EU grants and public procurement coexist.
claims.gap: Not every contractual term or beneficiary subgrant is public.

claims.claim: Some public programs explicitly finance counter-speech, hate-speech reporting, disinformation detection/analysis, resilience campaigns and media-literacy outputs.
claims.gap: These objectives do not by themselves prove censorship of lawful political speech.

claims.claim: Selection, financial reporting and evaluation requirements are materially documented, so state support is accompanied by administrative gatekeeping and accountability mechanisms.
claims.gap: Formal controls do not prove perfect neutrality or effectiveness.

claims.claim: The examined corpus does not establish a general chain public funder -> funded actor -> mandated removal of specific lawful political content -> political/electoral effect.
claims.gap: Case-specific contracts, instructions or platform workflows could change the responsibility assessment if produced.

controls.control: French and EU instruments document explicit eligibility, objectives, budgets and reporting/evaluation requirements rather than unrestricted transfers.
Public funding uses distinct legal/administrative vehicles, including grants, decentralised subsidies, multi-year agreements and procurement; these vehicles should not be conflated.

Several programs expressly support counter-speech, reporting of online hate, disinformation detection, media literacy or resilience, so public funding can shape the category of eligible activity and organisational capacity.
Selection and monitoring mechanisms are documented in DILCRAH, FIPD and EMI calls, limiting the inference that grants are uncontrolled transfers.
The examined public documents establish programmatic objectives and deliverables, not a general public-authority command chain over specific editorial conclusions or lawful-content removals.
No examined source closes the high causal chain from public grant or contract to voter persuasion or counterfactual electoral outcome.

facts.subject: DILCRAH national 2025 budget
facts.value: The DILCRAH 2025 national call allocated €7.7 million to support associations, a 7% increase from the previous year.

facts.subject: DILCRAH eligible entities
facts.value: The DILCRAH national call was open to non-profit legal persons including associations, public institutions, cultural institutions and educational institutions.

facts.subject: DILCRAH online-hate priorities
facts.value: DILCRAH priorities included production of alternative online speech and development of reporting of hate speech on the Internet.

facts.subject: DILCRAH selection and control
facts.value: Applications were instructed by DILCRAH and submitted to its grant-award commission; DILCRAH reserved the right to check the reality, effectiveness and alignment of funded actions.

facts.subject: DILCRAH durable and local support channels
facts.value: DILCRAH uses annual national and local calls and also multi-year objective agreements with major long-standing actors.

facts.subject: DILCRAH local 2025 envelope
facts.value: The 2025 local DILCRAH call had an envelope of €3 million and was fully decentralised to prefects.

facts.subject: DILCRAH local governance and financial follow-up
facts.value: Local calls use CORAH/CORAHD-type institutional review and require close scrutiny of financial reports and prior grant-use forms.

facts.subject: FIPD 2025 envelope
facts.value: The 2025 FIPD envelope managed and steered by SG-CIPDR was €52.7 million.

facts.subject: FIPD Programme R mission
facts.value: FIPD Programme R supports actions for prevention of radicalisation.

facts.subject: FIPD Programme R activity scope
facts.value: Programme R can fund counter-speech, public-awareness workshops, professional training, family support and other preventive actions; the call explicitly includes separatism, conspiracy phenomena and sectarian deviations.

facts.subject: FIPD grant framework
facts.value: The Paris 2025 FIPD call describes support as grants to project holders whose actions fit national prevention orientations.

facts.subject: Republican engagement condition
facts.value: Associations seeking FIPD grants must subscribe to the republican engagement contract, including commitments concerning constitutional principles, secularism and public order.

facts.subject: FIPD statutory purpose
facts.value: Article R132-4-1 of the Internal Security Code provides that FIPD finances delinquency-prevention and radicalisation-prevention actions.

facts.subject: FIPD allocation authority
facts.value: Article R132-4-2 provides that the interministerial committee sets orientations and eligibility conditions for FIPD credits and that credits are delegated to prefects.

facts.subject: Culture Ministry EMI grant mechanism
facts.value: The Ministry of Culture supports media and information literacy by allocating grants to project holders.

facts.subject: Culture Ministry EMI objective
facts.value: The stated EMI objective is to help citizens, especially young people, appropriate information and develop the freedom and capacity to form their own opinion.

facts.subject: DRAC EMI application evidence
facts.value: The Pays de la Loire EMI call requires a project description with target-person counts, timetable, planned media production, sustainability prospects and a full projected budget.

facts.subject: DRAC EMI monitoring indicators
facts.value: The same call requires monitoring and evaluation indicators for targeted publics, making reporting part of the grant-design rather than leaving outputs unspecified.

facts.subject: Creative Europe media literacy budget
facts.value: The 2024 cross-border media-literacy call had a €2.57 million budget, a maximum EU grant of €500,000 per two-year project and a 70% maximum co-financing rate.

facts.subject: Creative Europe eligible consortia
facts.value: The call required consortia of at least three entities from at least three participating countries and allowed non-profits, public authorities, universities, media organisations and technology providers among eligible participants.

facts.subject: Creative Europe expected deliverables
facts.value: Expected outputs included cross-border media-literacy tools/actions, exchange of best practices and support for media-literacy professionals.

facts.subject: EU 2025 resilience and reach calls
facts.value: The Commission launched two calls totalling nearly €5 million: €3.15 million for detecting/analyzing malicious manipulation and resilience responses, and about €1.6 million to increase reach and impact of independent fact-checked content.

facts.subject: EU 2025 eligible civil-society/research actors
facts.value: Civil-society organisations, universities and research centres were among eligible applicants, and winning projects were expected to collaborate with EDMO.

facts.subject: EDMO uses both procurement and grants
facts.value: EDMO central has been financed through public procurement while national/regional hubs have been financed through grants, so procurement and subsidy are distinct vehicles inside the same ecosystem.

facts.subject: EDMO funding is materially recurrent
facts.value: Commission figures list €2.5m then €4m procurement for EDMO central, about €11m for the first eight hubs, €8m for six additional hubs and further refinancing rounds.

facts.subject: EU youth information-integrity call
facts.value: A €6 million Commission call was designed to fund two projects involving young Europeans and influencers on manipulation techniques, conspiracy theories and malicious uses of generative AI/deepfakes.

facts.subject: CERV funds civil-society anti-hate capacity
facts.value: The CERV Equality 2025 call includes support for civil-society projects combating racism and hate, including awareness, victim support, data collection and resilience activities.

facts.subject: Funding documents do not themselves establish content-removal command
facts.value: Across the examined DILCRAH, FIPD, EMI, Creative Europe, EDMO and CERV instruments, public documents define eligibility, objectives, deliverables, reporting or evaluation; they do not by themselves establish a general instruction chain from funder to removal of specific lawful political content.

leads.evidence_excerpt: Recurring French and EU instruments finance anti-hate, radicalisation-prevention, media-literacy and disinformation-resilience capacity through several vehicles.
leads.gap: Complete beneficiary-level market map, concentration, renewal rates and outcome metrics remain incomplete.
leads.lead: Publicly financed counter-influence ecosystem as an economy of programs, grants and procurement

leads.evidence_excerpt: Program objectives and reporting are documented; a general instruction chain to specific lawful-content removal or electoral effect is not.
leads.gap: Need contracts/instructions/workflow records and causal exposure-outcome data.
leads.lead: Funding/capacity to command, removal and political effect
